title: Seeing Green: why cleantech failed and what a definite energy bet would need (CS183 Class 14)
summary: Thiel uses the cleantech bust to review his startup checklist: markets, competition, secrets, incrementalism, durability, teams, distribution, timing, financing and luck. He argues energy follows a power law, so a definite, optimistic bet (he sketches thorium) beats the indeterminate portfolio thinking that sank Solyndra-style ventures.

principles.text: Plans beat aspirations: a detailed plan gives mastery over luck; winning without one is hitting a jackpot.
principles.quote: But having a detailed plan is key. To be sure, there are some cases where things work despite the lack of a plan. But there is an awful lot of failure there too. Winning without a plan is hitting the jackpot, and most people do not hit the jackpot.

principles.text: Energy follows a power law: one source dominates, so portfolio thinking is a mistake.
principles.quote: Energy sources are probably not normally distributed in cost or effectiveness. There is probably one that is dramatically better than all others.

principles.text: You need good answers on all 10 startup questions; 8 of 10 is a B-, 5 of 10 is an F.
principles.quote: And, to reiterate, you really do need all 10; 8 out of 10 is sort of a B-, and 5 of 10 earns you an F.

principles.text: Huge, competitive markets breed mimetic competition and tiny profits; companies need a specific mission.
principles.quote: The economic insight is that the battles are so fierce because the stakes so small. Since profits are competed away, people are fighting over scraps.

principles.text: Long-horizon ventures need big secrets, and incremental improvements are not durable enough to win.
principles.quote: Secrets can allow you to escape mimesis and competition in a world of long time horizons, but those secrets need to be pretty big.

principles.text: Avoid investing in companies seeking under $1 million or over $1 billion, since power-law returns need plausible outsized growth.
principles.quote: A good, broad rule of thumb is to never invest in companies who are looking for less than $1 million or more than $1 billion.
